a.xlink:title: CNPG `instances: 2-3` answers AZ failover, not data protection — it survives a lost node or AZ, not a bad migration or a dropped table. A specific backup and restore strategy is an explicit non-goal of ADR-0007 and barman-to-S3 is unbuilt, so Longhorn's volume backups are today the only thing standing behind the Keycloak database. Moving it to gp3 removes that with nothing in its place.

a.xlink:title: The volume stays where it is either way; what per-AZ node groups (or Karpenter) buy is that "give me a node in this specific AZ" becomes an answerable request, so a rescheduled pod comes back as soon as its AZ has capacity — and when the AZ is what failed, it comes back with the AZ, rather than sitting in a pending state that reads like a storage bug. That is a documented topology fix, not a storage-layer one. The honest residual: if that AZ itself is gone, EBS-backed volumes are stranded until it returns, where Longhorn would usually reattach from a surviving replica — a real, priceable availability trade, not a blocker.

a.xlink:title: The strongest objection to removing Longhorn (Amit Kumar and Vini Cerutti, 2026-08-11): it is not only the RWX provider — as the sole default StorageClass it also hides that EBS volumes are AZ-bound.
a.text: the RWX provider — as the sole

a.xlink:title: The fix is documented but not free. One node group per AZ multiplies the node-group config surface by the number of zones — scaling bounds, instance types, taints, labels, and GPU variants replicated per zone — and each group scales independently, so headroom is per-AZ and utilisation drops. Karpenter avoids the fan-out by reading the PV's zone requirement natively, but replaces cluster-autoscaler, which is its own migration. Neither is exotic; both are more configuration than the single multi-AZ ASG NIC ships today, and that delta belongs in the comparison rather than in a footnote.

a.xlink:title: The residual is an availability trade, and its size depends on how often AZs fail and for how long. Full-AZ outages are infrequent and typically measured in hours, recovery needs no operator action — the volumes are intact and the pods reschedule when capacity returns — and the workload is interactive analysis rather than a customer-facing service, where the tolerable answer may simply be that affected users cannot work until the AZ is back. Two things keep this from being free: Nebari has no stated availability objective to check it against, so "acceptable" is currently a preference rather than a finding; and the services that genuinely should survive a lost AZ are databases, which the anecdotes do not transfer puts on CNPG replication rather than on the storage layer. Note also that Longhorn's own survival here is softer than assumed — NIC sets replica zone anti-affinity to soft with two replicas, so both can sit in the AZ that just failed.

a.xlink:title: The RWX-homes shape dissolves the objection rather than answering it: FSx for OpenZFS Multi-AZ presents a floating endpoint with automatic failover to a standby in a second AZ (EFS is regional with a mount target per AZ and shares the property), so a home is reachable from any AZ, there is no AZ to be pinned to, and an AZ outage becomes AWS's failover problem rather than the cluster's.
